title: So much data, so little time: Using sequential data analysis to monitor behavioral changes
author: Walker
materials: Name Objects for Your Baby, and (

steps.title: Schedule three play sessions
steps.instruction: Arrange three 20‑minute interactive play sessions for each dyad, spaced approximately 2.5 weeks apart.

steps.title: Prepare play environment
steps.instruction: Provide a standard set of toys for each session and instruct dyads to play as they would at home; set up video recording equipment to capture the entire 20‑minute interaction.

steps.title: Record baseline Session 1
steps.instruction: Conduct the first 20‑minute session, record video, and treat this data as the baseline measure of infant‑caregiver interaction and caregiver responsiveness.

steps.title: Show caregiver instructional video
steps.instruction: At the end of Session 1, play a 10‑minute video titled “Improving Your Baby’s Language Skills” that presents four tips: (1) Be Positive and Patient, (2) Act Naturally, (3) Name Objects for Your Baby, (4) Practice. Include brief strategies after each tip; a mother and her 18‑month‑old son model tips 1 and 3.

steps.title: Instruct post‑video practice
steps.instruction: After the video, tell caregivers to talk to their infants and practice the demonstrated caregiving behaviors during everyday interactions.

steps.title: Record Sessions 2 and 3
steps.instruction: Conduct the second and third 20‑minute play sessions (approximately 2.5 weeks apart) without providing any additional caregiving information, and record each session.

steps.title: Compile video data
steps.instruction: Gather all video recordings from Sessions 1‑3 for each dyad; note that about 61 % of families (n = 14) completed all three sessions.

steps.title: Run repeating behavior analysis
steps.instruction: Using O’Connor’s SEQGROUPS SPSS syntax, perform lag‑1 repeating consecutive‑behavior analysis on all infant and caregiver behaviors to obtain frequencies and transitional probabilities (e.g., idv‑idv frequency = 1, transitional probability = 0.50).

substeps.instruction: Import coded behavior sequences into SPSS.
Apply SEQGROUPS syntax for repeating analysis.
Calculate frequency counts for each behavior pair.
Compute transitional probabilities for each pair.

steps.title: Run non‑repeating behavior analysis
steps.instruction: Using the same SEQGROUPS program, perform lag‑1 non‑repeating consecutive‑behavior analysis by collapsing consecutive identical behaviors before calculating frequencies and transitional probabilities (e.g., idv, idv, cdv, ion → idv, cdv, ion; idv‑idv frequency = 0, probability = 0).

substeps.instruction: Collapse consecutive repeats in the coded sequences.
Apply SEQGROUPS syntax for non‑repeating analysis.
Calculate frequencies and transitional probabilities for the collapsed sequences.

steps.title: Statistical comparison of sessions
steps.instruction: Conduct likelihood‑ratio chi‑square tests comparing Session 1 to Sessions 2/3 for both repeating and non‑repeating analyses; report χ², degrees of freedom, p‑values, and effect sizes.

substeps.instruction: For repeating analysis, compute χ² = 866.72, df = 156, p < 0.001.
For non‑repeating analysis, compute χ² = 843.14, df = 156, p < 0.001.
